title: The Unhedgeable Bet: What the Future Combat Systems Can Teach Us About Acquisition
gist: Two Navy officers compare Golden Dome — the US missile-defense 'system of systems' with cost estimates from $252 billion to $3.6 trillion — to the Army's Future Combat Systems, which burned ~$18 billion without fielding a vehicle. Golden Dome is better hedged (gated competitions, layers with standalone value), but its Joint Fires Network dependency and an all-or-nothing ~1,000-satellite boost-phase interceptor layer are unhedgeable, so an independent authority empowered to fail its final integration gate is needed.

themes.theme: Golden Dome scale and cost uncertainty

insights.claim: Golden Dome for America integrates space-based sensors, orbital interceptors, ground systems and a command network; its architecture is so closely held that the CBO cannot fully price it, with cost estimates ranging from $252 billion to $3.6 trillion.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude cost range makes Golden Dome a huge but highly uncertain revenue pool for space, interceptor and C2 contractors, and a fiscal wildcard.
insights.quote: cost estimates span from $252 billion to $3.6 trillion

insights.claim: Eighteen months after its founding executive order, Golden Dome broke ground on its first operational site.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Program has moved from concept to physical execution, supporting near-term contract flow.

insights.claim: Nearly all Golden Dome funding arrived as a lump-sum reconciliation outside annual budget review, and its delivery deadline is set by an administration's term rather than technical readiness.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Reduced annual congressional scrutiny lowers near-term cancellation risk but raises later cost-overrun and political-reversal risk after the administration ends.
insights.quote: The deadline is set by an administration’s term rather than technical readiness

insights.claim: The Army's Future Combat Systems spent roughly $18 billion over six years without fielding a single vehicle, making it the most expensive canceled program in Army history.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Benchmark for the downside of tightly coupled mega-programs — relevant precedent for Golden Dome contractors' revenue risk.
insights.locator: One of the last times the Department

insights.claim: Future Combat Systems failed because it made an unhedgeable bet: eighteen interdependent systems with no standalone value, designed around a C-130 weight limit that replaced armor with networked 'see and shoot first' protection that could not be tested until the whole force existed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Programs whose components lack standalone value carry binary outcomes; prefer contractors on severable, independently valuable layers.
insights.quote: It failed because it made an unhedgeable bet on unproven, interdependent systems with no standalone value that couldn’t be abandoned once disproven.
insights.locator: One of the last times the Department

insights.claim: Future Combat Systems' network depended on the Joint Tactical Radio System, a separate program outside the Army's budget; when the radio struggled, the Army could neither replace the network nor field the force without it.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Dependency on externally owned enabling programs is a key failure vector to monitor in system-of-systems contracts.
insights.locator: The Promise and Peril of Interdependence

insights.claim: Three properties made Future Combat Systems unhedgeable: testing required the entire architecture at once, it could not be de-scoped because dropping a system forced software rewrites across dependents, and the expedited schedule treated immature technologies as on-demand deliverables.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: A checklist for evaluating fragility of large defense programs and their contractors.
insights.locator: Why the Bet Could Not Be Hedged

insights.claim: Future Combat Systems survived years of auditor warnings (business case judged inadequate as early as 2006) because it was the Army's budget centerpiece and identity, sunk costs, and subcontracting spanning over 100 congressional districts, until Robert Gates canceled it in April 2009.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Political dispersion of subcontracts entrenches programs — cancellation risk stays low until an outsider with political will intervenes.

insights.claim: Unlike Future Combat Systems, Golden Dome's components have standalone value: THAAD and Patriot provide theater defense regardless, and missile-warning and tracking satellites are capabilities the Space Force already funds.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Demand for THAAD, Patriot and tracking satellites is robust even if Golden Dome integration falters — lower-risk exposure than integration bets.

insights.claim: Golden Dome's interceptor effort is a gated prize competition among twelve companies moving from component testing to prototype and on-orbit demonstration, with no production requests until capabilities are proven.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Twelve-way competition means space-interceptor revenue is uncertain per company until later gates; winners determined by demonstrations.

insights.claim: Fielding more Patriot and THAAD capacity is cheap to reverse and slowing it is not defensible, whereas constellation size and integration architecture decisions are hard to reverse and should not be made before validation.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Supports continued near-term buys of mature interceptors while signaling scrutiny on space-constellation and C2 commitments.
insights.locator: A missile-defense advocate will likely object

themes.theme: Unhedgeable risks: network and boost-phase constellation

insights.claim: Golden Dome's success depends on a new, yet-to-be-fielded command-and-control network, likely the Joint Fires Network, which fuses data with complex software and AI, is already facing fielding and training delays under Inspector General scrutiny, and has no publicly known alternative.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: The C2 network is the lynchpin risk; delays there would cascade across all layers — key milestone for investors to track.

insights.claim: Continuous boost-phase coverage requires a minimum constellation of about 1,000 specialized space-based interceptor satellites, so a partial constellation produces a coverage gap rather than partial coverage.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: The boost-phase layer is binary — a large satellite-production opportunity that could be abandoned entirely, not trimmed.
insights.quote: a partial constellation is not partial coverage but a gap

insights.claim: The Golden Dome program director testified that space-based interceptors would be dropped if cost and scalability targets are not met — an advance fold criterion whose durability once a constellation is under contract is uncertain.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Explicit cancellation risk for the space-based interceptor layer; watch unit-cost data at demonstration gates.

insights.claim: The Nunn-McCurdy cost tripwire measures individual program baselines rather than structural dependencies, and rarely stops anything: all but four of thirty-seven breaches between 2007 and 2016 were certified rather than curtailed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Statutory cost breaches are weak cancellation signals for defense programs.
insights.quote: All but four of the thirty-seven breaches between 2007 and 2016 were certified rather than acted on by curtailing the program.

insights.claim: The authors recommend committing cost and performance thresholds before Golden Dome gates and chartering a standing non-advocate review outside the program, drawing on DOT&E and CAPE, empowered to fail the final integration gate outright.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
entities: Director of Operational Test and Evaluation
insights.so_what: If adopted, introduces a credible late-stage cancellation mechanism, raising risk for integration-dependent contracts.

insights.claim: A program can pass technical demonstrations while unit costs drift high enough that the affordable fleet falls below the coverage threshold, passing gates yet failing to deliver capability.
insights.speaker: Andrew Tenbusch and Trevor Phillips-Levine
insights.so_what: Unit-cost trajectory of space interceptors is the key metric for viability, not just test success.
insights.locator: First, gate criteria should include cost
